title: Moral Injury
subtitle: Psychological impact of violating or witnessing deeply held values
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating moral injury across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain moral injury in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in moral injury.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to moral injury.

sections.explainSimply: Moral injury centres on guilt, shame, betrayal, anger and loss of meaning after morally injurious events.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: It can coexist with PTSD but is not reducible to fear circuitry or currently a standalone formal diagnosis.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Mechanistic research is early; social, spiritual and cultural dimensions are central and cannot be replaced by neurobiology.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of moral injury as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need moral injury to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not medicalise ethical conflict or bypass accountability and repair.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use moral injury to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses moral injury to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not medicalise ethical conflict or bypass accountability and repair. Evidence classification: emerging construct.
